&lt;p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:9pt;"&gt;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:6pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;The estimated fair value of Schlumberger&amp;#8217;s &lt;font style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Long-term Debt, &lt;/font&gt;based on quoted market prices at March 31, 2019 and December 31, 2018, was $16.7 billion and $14.6 billion, respectively. &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;At March 31, 2019, Schlumberger had separate committed credit facility agreements aggregating $6.5 billion with commercial banks, of which $3.8 billion was available and unused.&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;#160;These committed facilities support commercial paper programs in the United States and Europe, of which $1.0 billion matures in February 2020, &amp;#160;$1.5 billion matures in November 2020, $2.0 billion matures in February 2023 and $2.0 billion matures in February 2024.&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;Interest rates and other terms of borrowing under these lines of credit vary by facility. &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Borrowings under Schlumberger&amp;#8217;s commercial paper programs at March 31, 2019 and December 31, 2018 were $2.7 billion and $2.4 billion, respectively, all of which were classified in &lt;font style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Long-term Debt&lt;/font&gt; in the &lt;font style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Consolidated Balance Sheet&lt;/font&gt;.&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;In April 2019, Schlumberger completed a debt exchange offer, pursuant to which it issued $1.500 billion in principal of 3.90% Senior Notes due 2028 (the &amp;#8220;New Notes&amp;#8221;) in exchange for $401 million of 3.00% Senior Notes due 2020, $234 million of 3.63% Senior Notes due 2022 and $817 million of 4.00% Senior Notes due 2025.&amp;#160; In connection with the exchange of principal, Schlumberger paid a premium of $48 million, substantially all of which was in the form of New Notes.&amp;#160; This premium will be amortized as additional interest expense over the term of the New Notes.&lt;font style="color:#000000;"&gt; &lt;/font&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</us-gaap:LongTermDebtTextBlock>
  <us-gaap:DerivativeInstrumentsAndHedgingActivitiesDisclosureTextBlock id="F_000287" contextRef="C_0000087347_20190101_20190331">
&lt;p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;8.&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp; &lt;font style="text-decoration:underline;"&gt;Derivative Instruments and Hedging Activities&lt;/font&gt; &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:6pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Schlumberger is exposed to market risks related to fluctuations in foreign currency exchange rates and interest rates.&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;To mitigate these risks, Schlumberger utilizes derivative instruments.&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;Schlumberger does not enter into derivative transactions for speculative purposes. &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:18pt;text-indent:0%;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Interest Rate Risk &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:6pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Schlumberger is subject to interest rate risk on its debt and its investment portfolio.&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;Schlumberger maintains an interest rate risk management strategy that uses a mix of variable and fixed rate debt combined with its investment portfolio, and occasionally interest rate swaps, to mitigate the exposure to changes in interest rates.&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;During 2017, a Canadian-dollar functional currency subsidiary of Schlumberger issued $1.1 billion of US-dollar denominated debt.&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;Schlumberger entered into cross-currency swaps for an aggregate notional amount of $1.1 billion in order to hedge changes in the fair value of its $0.5 billion 2.20% Senior Notes due 2020 and its $0.6 billion 2.65% Senior Notes due 2022. These cross-currency swaps effectively convert the US-dollar notes to Canadian-dollar denominated debt with fixed annual interest rates of 1.97% and 2.52%, respectively.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;These cross-currency swaps are designated as cash flow hedges. The changes in the fair values of the hedges are recorded on the &lt;font style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Consolidated Balance Sheet &lt;/font&gt;and in &lt;font style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss. &lt;/font&gt;Amounts recorded in &lt;font style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss&lt;/font&gt; are reclassified to earnings in the same periods that the underlying hedged item is recognized in earnings.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;At March 31, 2019, Schlumberger had fixed rate debt aggregating $13.5 billion and variable rate debt aggregating $3.0 billion, after taking into account the effect of interest rate swaps. &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:18pt;text-indent:0%;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Foreign Currency Exchange Rate Risk &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:6pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;As a multinational company, Schlumberger generates revenue in more than 120 countries. Schlumberger&amp;#8217;s functional currency is primarily the US dollar.&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;However, outside the United States, a significant portion of Schlumberger&amp;#8217;s expenses is incurred in foreign currencies.&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;Therefore, when the US dollar weakens (strengthens) in relation to the foreign currencies of the countries in which Schlumberger conducts business, the US dollar-reported expenses will increase (decrease).&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp; &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Schlumberger is exposed to risks on future cash flows to the extent that the local currency is not the functional currency and expenses denominated in local currency are not equal to revenues denominated in local currency.&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;Schlumberger is also exposed to risks on future cash flows relating to certain of its fixed rate debt denominated in currencies other than the functional currency.&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;Schlumberger uses foreign currency forward contracts to provide a hedge against a portion of these cash flow risks.&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;These contracts are accounted for as cash flow hedges, with the changes in the fair value of the hedge recorded on the &lt;font style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Consolidated Balance Sheet &lt;/font&gt;and in &lt;font style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss.&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/font&gt;Amounts recorded in&lt;font style="font-style:italic;"&gt; Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss &lt;/font&gt;are reclassified into earnings in the same period or periods that the hedged item is recognized in earnings.&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;At March 31, 2019, Schlumberger recognized a cumulative net $16 million loss in &lt;font style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss&lt;/font&gt; relating to revaluation of foreign currency forward contracts designated as cash flow hedges, the majority of which is expected to be reclassified into earnings within the next 12 months. &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Schlumberger is exposed to changes in the fair value of assets and liabilities that are denominated in currencies other than the functional currency.&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;While Schlumberger uses foreign currency forward contracts and foreign currency options to economically hedge this exposure as it relates to certain currencies, these contracts are not designated as hedges for accounting purposes.&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;Instead, the fair value of the contracts is recorded on the &lt;font style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Consolidated Balance Sheet, &lt;/font&gt;and changes in the fair value are recognized in the &lt;font style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Consolidated Statement of Income &lt;/font&gt;as are changes in fair value of the hedged item. &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;At March 31, 2019, contracts were outstanding for the US dollar equivalent of $4.0 billion in various foreign currencies, of which $1.1 billion relates to hedges of debt denominated in currencies other than the functional currency. &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;The effect of derivative instruments designated as fair value and cash flow hedges, and those not designated as hedges, on the &lt;font style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Consolidated Statement of Income&lt;/font&gt; was as follows: &lt;/p&gt;

<a href="javascript:void(0);" onclick="top.Show.toggleNext( this );">- Definition</a><div><p>Total of all stockholders' equity (deficit) items, net of receivables from officers, directors, owners, and affiliates of the entity which are attributable to the parent. The amount of the economic entity's stockholders' equity attributable to the parent excludes the amount of stockholders' equity which is allocable to that ownership interest in subsidiary equity which is not attributable to the parent (noncontrolling interest, minority interest). <p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:2pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Amortization expense charged to income was $160 million during the first quarter of 2019 and $165 million during the first quarter of 2018.</p>
<p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:2pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</p>
<p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Based on the net book value of intangible assets at March 31, 2019, amortization charged to income for the subsequent five years is estimated to be: remaining three quarters of 2019&#8212;$510 million; 2020&#8212;$657 million; 2021&#8212;$628 million; 2022&#8212;$622 million; 2023&#8212;$609 million; and 2024&#8212;$563 million. </p><span></span>
</td>
</tr>

<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:6pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">The estimated fair value of Schlumberger&#8217;s <font style="font-style:italic;">Long-term Debt, </font>based on quoted market prices at March 31, 2019 and December 31, 2018, was $16.7 billion and $14.6 billion, respectively. </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">At March 31, 2019, Schlumberger had separate committed credit facility agreements aggregating $6.5 billion with commercial banks, of which $3.8 billion was available and unused.&nbsp;&nbsp;&#160;These committed facilities support commercial paper programs in the United States and Europe, of which $1.0 billion matures in February 2020, &#160;$1.5 billion matures in November 2020, $2.0 billion matures in February 2023 and $2.0 billion matures in February 2024.&nbsp;&nbsp;Interest rates and other terms of borrowing under these lines of credit vary by facility. </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Borrowings under Schlumberger&#8217;s commercial paper programs at March 31, 2019 and December 31, 2018 were $2.7 billion and $2.4 billion, respectively, all of which were classified in <font style="font-style:italic;">Long-term Debt</font> in the <font style="font-style:italic;">Consolidated Balance Sheet</font>.&nbsp;&nbsp;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">In April 2019, Schlumberger completed a debt exchange offer, pursuant to which it issued $1.500 billion in principal of 3.90% Senior Notes due 2028 (the &#8220;New Notes&#8221;) in exchange for $401 million of 3.00% Senior Notes due 2020, $234 million of 3.63% Senior Notes due 2022 and $817 million of 4.00% Senior Notes due 2025.&#160; In connection with the exchange of principal, Schlumberger paid a premium of $48 million, substantially all of which was in the form of New Notes.&#160; This premium will be amortized as additional interest expense over the term of the New Notes.<font style="color:#000000;"> </font></p><span></span>

<th class="tl" colspan="1" rowspan="2"><div style="width: 200px;"><strong>Derivative Instruments and Hedging Activities<br></strong></div></th>
<th class="th" colspan="1">3 Months Ended</th>
</tr>
<tr><th class="th"><div>Mar. 31, 2019</div></th></tr>
<tr class="re">
<td class="pl " style="border-bottom: 0px;" valign="top"><a class="a" href="javascript:void(0);" onclick="top.Show.showAR( this, 'defref_us-gaap_DerivativeInstrumentsAndHedgingActivitiesDisclosureAbstract', window );"><strong>Derivative Instruments And Hedging Activities Disclosure [Abstract]</strong></a></td>
<td class="text">&#160;<span></span>
</td>
</tr>
<tr class="ro">
<td class="pl " style="border-bottom: 0px;" valign="top"><a class="a" href="javascript:void(0);" onclick="top.Show.showAR( this, 'defref_us-gaap_DerivativeInstrumentsAndHedgingActivitiesDisclosureTextBlock', window );">Derivative Instruments and Hedging Activities</a></td>
<td class="text">
<p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">8.&nbsp;&nbsp; <font style="text-decoration:underline;">Derivative Instruments and Hedging Activities</font> </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:6pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Schlumberger is exposed to market risks related to fluctuations in foreign currency exchange rates and interest rates.&nbsp;&nbsp;To mitigate these risks, Schlumberger utilizes derivative instruments.&nbsp;&nbsp;Schlumberger does not enter into derivative transactions for speculative purposes. </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:18pt;text-indent:0%;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Interest Rate Risk </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:6pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Schlumberger is subject to interest rate risk on its debt and its investment portfolio.&nbsp;&nbsp;Schlumberger maintains an interest rate risk management strategy that uses a mix of variable and fixed rate debt combined with its investment portfolio, and occasionally interest rate swaps, to mitigate the exposure to changes in interest rates.&nbsp;&nbsp;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">During 2017, a Canadian-dollar functional currency subsidiary of Schlumberger issued $1.1 billion of US-dollar denominated debt.&nbsp;&nbsp;Schlumberger entered into cross-currency swaps for an aggregate notional amount of $1.1 billion in order to hedge changes in the fair value of its $0.5 billion 2.20% Senior Notes due 2020 and its $0.6 billion 2.65% Senior Notes due 2022. These cross-currency swaps effectively convert the US-dollar notes to Canadian-dollar denominated debt with fixed annual interest rates of 1.97% and 2.52%, respectively.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">These cross-currency swaps are designated as cash flow hedges. The changes in the fair values of the hedges are recorded on the <font style="font-style:italic;">Consolidated Balance Sheet </font>and in <font style="font-style:italic;">Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss. </font>Amounts recorded in <font style="font-style:italic;">Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss</font> are reclassified to earnings in the same periods that the underlying hedged item is recognized in earnings.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">At March 31, 2019, Schlumberger had fixed rate debt aggregating $13.5 billion and variable rate debt aggregating $3.0 billion, after taking into account the effect of interest rate swaps. </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:18pt;text-indent:0%;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Foreign Currency Exchange Rate Risk </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:6pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">As a multinational company, Schlumberger generates revenue in more than 120 countries. Schlumberger&#8217;s functional currency is primarily the US dollar.&nbsp;&nbsp;However, outside the United States, a significant portion of Schlumberger&#8217;s expenses is incurred in foreign currencies.&nbsp;&nbsp;Therefore, when the US dollar weakens (strengthens) in relation to the foreign currencies of the countries in which Schlumberger conducts business, the US dollar-reported expenses will increase (decrease).&nbsp;&nbsp; </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Schlumberger is exposed to risks on future cash flows to the extent that the local currency is not the functional currency and expenses denominated in local currency are not equal to revenues denominated in local currency.&nbsp;&nbsp;Schlumberger is also exposed to risks on future cash flows relating to certain of its fixed rate debt denominated in currencies other than the functional currency.&nbsp;&nbsp;Schlumberger uses foreign currency forward contracts to provide a hedge against a portion of these cash flow risks.&nbsp;&nbsp;These contracts are accounted for as cash flow hedges, with the changes in the fair value of the hedge recorded on the <font style="font-style:italic;">Consolidated Balance Sheet </font>and in <font style="font-style:italic;">Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss.&nbsp;&nbsp;</font>Amounts recorded in<font style="font-style:italic;"> Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss </font>are reclassified into earnings in the same period or periods that the hedged item is recognized in earnings.&nbsp;&nbsp;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">At March 31, 2019, Schlumberger recognized a cumulative net $16 million loss in <font style="font-style:italic;">Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss</font> relating to revaluation of foreign currency forward contracts designated as cash flow hedges, the majority of which is expected to be reclassified into earnings within the next 12 months. </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Schlumberger is exposed to changes in the fair value of assets and liabilities that are denominated in currencies other than the functional currency.&nbsp;&nbsp;While Schlumberger uses foreign currency forward contracts and foreign currency options to economically hedge this exposure as it relates to certain currencies, these contracts are not designated as hedges for accounting purposes.&nbsp;&nbsp;Instead, the fair value of the contracts is recorded on the <font style="font-style:italic;">Consolidated Balance Sheet, </font>and changes in the fair value are recognized in the <font style="font-style:italic;">Consolidated Statement of Income </font>as are changes in fair value of the hedged item. </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">At March 31, 2019, contracts were outstanding for the US dollar equivalent of $4.0 billion in various foreign currencies, of which $1.1 billion relates to hedges of debt denominated in currencies other than the functional currency. </p>
<p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">The effect of derivative instruments designated as fair value and cash flow hedges, and those not designated as hedges, on the <font style="font-style:italic;">Consolidated Statement of Income</font> was as follows: </p>
<p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</p>

<tr><td class="hide"><a style="color: white;" href="javascript:void(0);" onclick="top.Show.hideAR();">X</a></td></tr>
<tr><td><div class="body" style="padding: 2px;">
<a href="javascript:void(0);" onclick="top.Show.toggleNext( this );">- Definition</a><div><p>The entire disclosure for loss and gain contingencies. Describes any existing condition, situation, or set of circumstances involving uncertainty as of the balance sheet date (or prior to issuance of the financial statements) as to a probable or reasonably possible loss incurred by an entity that will ultimately be resolved when one or more future events occur or fail to occur, and typically discloses the amount of loss recorded or a range of possible loss, or an assertion that no reasonable estimate can be made.</p></div>

<a href="javascript:void(0);" onclick="top.Show.toggleNext( this );">- Definition</a><div><p>The entire disclosure for reporting segments including data and tables. Reportable segments include those that meet any of the following quantitative thresholds a) it's reported revenue, including sales to external customers and intersegment sales or transfers is 10 percent or more of the combined revenue, internal and external, of all operating segments b) the absolute amount of its reported profit or loss is 10 percent or more of the greater, in absolute amount of 1) the combined reported profit of all operating segments that did not report a loss or 2) the combined reported loss of all operating segments that did report a loss c) its assets are 10 percent or more of the combined assets of all operating segments.</p></div>

<table border="0" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" class="authRefData" style="display: none;" id="defref_us-gaap_AmortizationOfIntangibleAssets">
<tr><td class="hide"><a style="color: white;" href="javascript:void(0);" onclick="top.Show.hideAR();">X</a></td></tr>
<tr><td><div class="body" style="padding: 2px;">
<a href="javascript:void(0);" onclick="top.Show.toggleNext( this );">- Definition</a><div><p>The aggregate expense charged against earnings to allocate the cost of intangible assets (nonphysical assets not used in production) in a systematic and rational manner to the periods expected to benefit from such assets. As a noncash expense, this element is added back to net income when calculating cash provided by or used in operations using the indirect method.</p></div>

<tr><td><div class="body" style="padding: 2px;">
<a href="javascript:void(0);" onclick="top.Show.toggleNext( this );">- Definition</a><div><p>Amount, excluding tax collected from customer, of revenue from satisfaction of performance obligation by transferring promised good or service to customer. Tax collected from customer is tax assessed by governmental authority that is both imposed on and concurrent with specific revenue-producing transaction, including, but not limited to, sales, use, value added and excise.</p></div>
